Header: 2026-07-21 14:30 UTC | Duration: 42 min | Recording: yes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Ethan Brooks (Redwood Security PM); Sofia Reynolds (CISO, Alderbrook), Liam Hart (Head Cloud Eng), Priya Nair (Legal), Tomás Vega (Infra)
---
Summary (auto): quick security + data residency deep-dive focused on KMS boundary, cross-border routing, and sub-processor transparency. Customer wants BYOK, clear region pinning, and assurance around SCCs / transfer mechanisms.
Topics (auto): KMS/BYOK, region pinning, sub-processors, SOC2/ISO evidence, DPA updates, fallback routing.

00:00 Jordan: ok great, thanks everyone for joining, we'll run through our security boundary and specifically the kms bring-your-own-key story and how region pinning works for eu vs us tenants.
00:14 Sofia: thanks, I'm Sofia, CISO at Alderbrook, high level we need to ensure no eu personal data leaves the eu for processing, except with explicit legal basis, and we need an auditable chain for keys.
00:30 Maya: absolutely, and we can start with the high-level modes — hosted api, dedicated, private — and then map the kms options to those. just to check, are you evaluating hosted or private?
00:45 Liam: priority is hosted with VPC peering or dedicated reserve. We want to avoid on-prem unless required. main ask is BYOK and firm region pinning for eu customers.
01:00 Ethan: quick callout, our platform supports BYOK via customer-managed keys in both aws kms and azure key vault, we also have hsm-backed options. in hosted mode keys can be stored in your ksm? sorry kms with a dedicated tenant so redwood never sees plaintext keys.
01:20 Tomás: small note — what happens when we have to failover to a us region due to capacity? that was the scenario that raised alarms. we need predictable behaviour.
01:36 Maya: good question, by default we route to the pinned region, but we have fallback policies. for customers with strict residency you can opt into hard region pinning which disables cross-region fallback. that is an enterprise option — it affects latency/availability tradeoffs.
01:58 Priya: and legally we need to know subprocessors in all regions and whether they can access the key materials. can you promise that subprocessors won't hold keys?
02:12 Ethan: we can confirm sub-processors do not have access to customer-managed key material. we use envelope encryption — tokens encrypted with customer key when BYOK is used — redwood only holds ciphertext. subprocessors provide runtime capacity but never unwrapped keys.
02:36 Sofia: can you describe the envelope flow in the eu context, like azure region eu-west, do you do any cross-region caching of kv caches or prefixes that might trigger egress?
02:55 Maya: we do prefix caching to speed up inference; by default cache nodes are co-located in the same region as the runtime when region pinning is active. for hosted eu tenants we pin cache and kv to eu datacenters. the mis-translation sometimes in docs calls this "kv cash" — sorry human transcript — but it's really key value cache.
03:18 Liam: documentation? we reviewed a doc that said some background processes communicate with control plane in us-west, is that a hard requirement?
03:29 Jordan: our control plane is multi-region but currently some telemetry and control-plane operations originate from us regions. for customers needing full control we have a private control-plane option where those calls are routed through your vpc and the control plane endpoints sit in your region.
03:44 Priya: legal will need the DPA amendment that lists that private control plane option and clarifies where logs live and who has admin access.
03:55 Ethan: yeah, and for auditability — we produce immutable audit logs per token, per request. logs can be retained in your storage for the retention window you select; for private deployments we can push logs directly to your S3/Blob storage inside eu.
04:18 Sofia: what about SCCs and transfer mechanisms — we operate under eu gdpr, we can't rely on vague statements. we need the mechanism spelled out if any data crosses to the us.
04:32 Jordan: we support standard contractual clauses (formerly sccs) and updated dpas. also we offer data processor addendum with clear sub-processor list. for customers who cannot accept SCCs we advise private deployment in eu or on-prem.
04:47 Tomás: is there any case where metadata or model telemetry goes out of eu even with region pinning?
04:56 Maya: minimal telemetry hits our global control plane by default, but again private control plane removes that. we can also redact or disable telemetry for regulated workloads.
05:08 Liam: ok, back to keys — BYOK flow: we give you a key identifier, the runtime calls your kms to unwrap per-request material? can we see a diagram?
05:22 Maya: yes, brief: client upload or create key in your KMS; you grant Redwood's service principal limited decrypt rights; at runtime the inference host requests ephemeral data keys from your KMS, KMS returns data key encrypted under your master key, Redwood uses the encrypted data key (never it unwrapped unless you give decrypt permission) — i'm trying to keep it plain but transcripts mess up technical words.
05:52 Sofia: pause — that sounds like a potential leak: where do ephemeral keys live and who has decrypt rights? we can't give broad long-term decrypt rights to third parties.
06:05 Ethan: we recommend a short-lived grant — we use conditional grants and can rotate auth principals. also HSM integrations limit operations. plus we maintain an approval workflow for push grants so you can see each service principal bind.
06:22 Priya: id like that in writing — is the approval workflow supported programmatically? we need proof for the audit.
06:30 Jordan: yes, we can provide a runbook and a sample terraform module that shows granting and revoking ephemeral decrypt rights. Maya will share the module.
06:40 Maya: noted, i'll include that. also, we have an option called key-escrow for customers who prefer us to hold wrapped keys in a secondary geo — but that is only by agreement and requires additional compliance steps.
06:58 Sofia: escrow is a non-starter for us. we need BYOK without Redwood escrow.
07:05 Jordan: understood. that matches many financial customers.
07:12 Liam: one more nuance: what about embeddings and storing derived vectors? they might be considered personal data. can you pin storage of embeddings to EU?
07:24 Maya: yes, embeddings and any persisted artifacts can be pinned. we expose per-route config to choose storage region and retention policy. default for eu tenants is eu.
07:38 Tomás: and encryption at rest keys for persisted artifacts — are those using the same BYOK?
07:45 Ethan: yes you can use your KMS to protect persisted stores as well. we support envelope encryption for DB and blob stores.
07:55 Sofia: SOC 2 and ISO — we need to see the last reports, scope, and any residual exceptions. we will ask for redacted SOC 2 type 2 and iso cert, and scope including data flow maps.
08:08 Jordan: Ethan will share SOC 2 type II redacted and ISO27001 summary after call.
08:14 Priya: also share pen test summary and remediation timelines.
08:19 Ethan: will do.

08:35 Liam: what about sub-processor list — we need names, locations, and purpose. also whether any sub-processors are in US or third countries.
08:48 Jordan: our standard sub-processor list includes cloud infra providers (aws, azure, gcp), monitoring providers, and a small set of edge cache partners. we'll give you the full inventory and the region mapping.
09:00 Priya: and we need contractual commitments that sub-processors will not re-subcontract or will be named.
09:09 Jordan: we include that in the DPA; you can also request a sub-processor addendum if you need additional contractual language.
09:18 Sofia: ok, how does region pinning work when customers have dual-operational footprint? say we have EU customers and US customers under same bank — can you partition by route?
09:32 Maya: yes, per-tenant or per-route pinning is supported. you can route eu user traffic to eu clusters and us traffic to us clusters; we support geo-affinity rules and header-based routing.
09:44 Tomás: curious about session affinity and kv cache — are session tokens stored cross-region for performance?
09:54 Maya: session tokens are stored regionally by default; cross-region replication is disabled for hard pinning. soft pinning allows replication for availability.
10:08 Priya: if we opt for hard pinning, what SLA impact — we can't accept silent failures during failovers.
10:18 Jordan: hard pinning increases the chance of capacity-related errors in the rare event of regional outage; for mission-critical we recommend Dedicated with reserved capacity or Private deployment inside eu. both have strong SLA options.
10:30 Sofia: price tradeoffs? not in this call but it's relevant — if dedicated is the recommendation we will need cost estimates.
10:38 Jordan: we'll follow up with pricing.

10:48 Maya: quick demo pointer — we'll show a small terraform sample today, but i propose a deeper KMS lab next week where you can test grant revocation in your sandbox.
10:58 Liam: yes please. make it a hands-on lab.
11:03 Priya: legal will review the redacted dpa and the sub-processor list — once we see it, we might request minor wording changes.
11:12 Jordan: understood. we'll send updated DPA and sub-processor inventory to Priya and Sofia.
11:20 Ethan: one more technical point: for telemetry and trace data that we keep for observability, we can disable PII collection or hash it client-side before transmitting to control plane. that is an opt-in config.
11:36 Sofia: good — we will want hashing client-side and retention window of 90 days or less.
11:44 Jordan: noted.

11:52 Maya: recap of next steps: share DPA and sub-processor list; schedule KMS lab; send SOC2/ISO docs; provide terraform sample for ephemeral grant. anything else?
12:05 Sofia: add pen test summary and example of audit logs exported to our s3.
12:12 Jordan: we'll include that. thanks everyone. we'll follow up with calendar invites for the lab.
12:20 End of recording.
